The words

Who can describe the joys that rise
Thro' all the courts of Paradise
To see a prodigal return,
To see an heir of glory born?

With joy the Father doth approve
The fruit of his eternal love;
The Son with joy looks down and sees
The purchase of his agonies.

The Spirit takes delight to view
The holy soul he form'd anew;
And saints and angels join to sing
The growing empire of their King.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum E and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (E), on the word “Who”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Isaac Watts wrote these words for his Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707), Book I, collected from the Scriptures, hymn 101, headed “Joy in heaven for a repenting sinner, Luke 15. 7-10”.

Watts' hymns were printed without tunes and sung to any tune of their metre, Long Metre (8.8.8.8). This page sets the words to UXBRIDGE; any other Long Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Words (1707): Isaac Watts (1674–1748)
  • Music (1830): Lowell Mason (1792–1872)

Tune UXBRIDGE by Lowell Mason (1792–1872); words by Isaac Watts (1674–1748).

Sung to the same tune: 'Twas by an Order from the Lord, Behold the Blind Their Sight Receive, Do We Not Know That Solemn Word, Glory to God the Trinity, Great Was the Day, the Joy Was Great, Had I the Tongues of Greeks and Jews, Here at Thy Cross, My Dying God, High on a Hill of Dazzling Light, In Gabriel's Hand a Mighty Stone, Jesus Is Gone Above the Skies, Life Is the Time to Serve the Lord, Lord, We Are Blind, We Mortals Blind, Man Has a Soul of Vast Desires, No More, My God, I Boast No More, Now Have Our Hearts Embrac'd Our God, Now in the Heat of Youthful Blood, Often I Seek My Lord by Night, Questions and Doubts Be Heard No More, Thus Far the Lord Has Led Me on, Thy Favours Lord, Surprise Our Souls, Up to the Fields Where Angels Lie.

Questions about Who Can Describe the Joys That Rise

What is the doh of Who Can Describe the Joys That Rise?

In this version, in E major, doh is E. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Who Can Describe the Joys That Rise start on?

It starts on d (E in E major), a pickup on the word “Who” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is Who Can Describe the Joys That Rise in the public domain?

Yes. Isaac Watts died in 1748, Lowell Mason died in 1872; the words were first published in 1707 and the music in 1830. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
